summary: Ensign in the Orange County, New York militia and John's only proven Revolutionary patriot, who went on to pioneer Plymouth and Jackson Township, Pennsylvania; John's 6th-great-grandfather.
bio:
Thomas Lamoreaux was born about 1745 in Orange County, New York, of Huguenot stock: the family had left France after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. His parents were probably Jean, or John, Lamoreaux (1723–1809) and Charity Davenport; the Sons of the American Revolution accepted that descent in 2017, though the 1919 Lamoureux family record leaves him in either John's or his brother Peter's family. He married Keturah Tuttle, daughter of John Tuthill and Temperance Smith.

In 1775 he signed the Articles of Association in Cornwall Precinct, Orange County, alongside James Tuttle, probably his wife's brother. In 1776 he was ensign of the Woodbury Clove militia company under Captain Francis Smith, very probably his wife's uncle, in the regiment of Colonel Woodhull, very probably Colonel Jesse Woodhull, a cousin of Keturah. For this service he is recognised as a patriot ancestor by both the Sons and the Daughters of the American Revolution, and he is John's only proven Revolutionary patriot. A family tradition that he was held on a Long Island prison ship is unverified, and his grave marker's description of him as a private of the War of 1812, when he would have been about 67, probably refers to a son.

In the spring of 1790 he moved his family to Plymouth, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, so they had not been in the Wyoming Valley for the massacre of 1778, and by that October he was serving in Captain George P. Ransom's militia company. Before 1800 he and Thomas Case led the pioneers who "scaled the northern wall of the valley, the Shawnee mountain" and settled in Jackson Township at Chase. The stone walls on their two farms were "a matter of marvel in early days", and one of his six sons was long remembered for the number of feet of wall he laid in a day.

His will, made on 15 April 1815 with a codicil of 1826, shows a stern father: he disinherited his son James "on account of his disobedience to me" while giving James's crippled son Jewel a share equal to his daughters', cut his son John down to fifty dollars in view of "the privileges already he has had", cut out Thomas Jr. for "interference and bad conduct" and gave that share to a grandson, Wesley, and left his wife Keturah his "best horse saddle & bridle" and one hundred dollars. He died in 1829 in Jackson Township. One record places his burial at Shupp's Cemetery, Larksville, but the family burying ground is on the old Lamoreaux farm at Chase, Tilling Point Farm, where the DAR placed a marker in 2017. Five descendants have joined the SAR through his sons James, Thomas and Daniel; none has yet done so through his daughter Martha Pringle, John's ancestress, so John's would be a new line.

researchNotes:
Thomas Lamoreaux was born about 1745 (SAR supplemental application gives c.1745-1829; tree 1746-1829), of Huguenot descent (Harvey Book p.135: the family descended from Huguenots who left France after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes). His parents were probably Jean (John) Lamoreaux (1723-1809) and Charity Davenport; the SAR approved a 2017 supplemental application tracing patriot John Lamoreaux to Thomas, though the 1919 Lamoureux Record leaves Thomas in either John's or Peter's family. In 1775 he signed the Articles of Association in Cornwall Precinct, Orange Co., alongside 'James Tuttle' (probably his wife's brother). In 1776 he was ensign of the Woodbury Clove company ('Thos. Lammoreux, ensign') under Capt. Francis Smith - very probably his wife Keturah's uncle - in the regiment of Colonel Woodhull, very probably Col. Jesse Woodhull, a cousin of Keturah. He is SAR Patriot P-232580 and DAR ancestor A068239. He married Keturah Tuttle. In spring 1790 he moved to Plymouth, Luzerne Co., and by October 1790 served in Capt. George P. Ransom's militia company (Harvey Book p.355) - so the family was not in the valley for the 1778 Wyoming Massacre. With Thomas Case he headed the pioneers who 'scaled the northern wall of the valley, the Shawnee mountain' before 1800, settling in Jackson Twp; 'the vast extent and character of the stone wall upon the farms of these two old settlers were a matter of marvel in early days... the miles of it to-day... are a monument of the toil', and one of his six sons was pointed out 'for having laid so many feet of stone wall in a day' (Wright pp.399-400). His will (15 Apr 1815, codicil 9 Nov 1826, registered 5 Oct 1829, Luzerne Will Book A pp.341-3) disinherited son James 'on account of his disobedience to me', gave James's crippled son Jewel ('Jewel Lamoreaux a cripple child') a share equal with his daughters, cut son John's bequest to $50 'considering... the privileges already he has had', cut Thomas Jr. out for 'interference and bad conduct' (his share to grandson Wesley), and left wife Keturah his 'best horse saddle & bridle' and $100. Burial: the SAR record says Shupp's Cemetery, Larksville; the family burying ground is on the Lamoreaux farm at Chase, Jackson Twp (Tilling Point Farm), where a DAR marker was placed in 2017. His Find a Grave grave marker calls him a War of 1812 private - he would have been about 67, so this is possibly his son. WikiTree's tradition that he was held on a Long Island prison ship is unverified. All three approved SAR applications (1995, 2014, 2017) descend through his sons James or Thomas, none through Martha.

The SAR Patriot Research System entry P-232580 now shows five approved member applications: three already known (1995, 2014, 2017) and two approved in late 2025 - Joshua Paul Lance (NJ, 10 Oct 2025, via son James) and Brian Tyler Baker (PA, 7 Nov 2025, via son Daniel) ([R4-S1]). None descends through Martha (Pringle), so Johnny's line would be a new line for SAR/DAR; the existing applications can be bought from SAR for their proofs of Thomas's service. The SAR page records burial at Shupp's Cemetery, Larksville, but notes 'No entry found in Find-A-Grave - Nov 2024'.

The page also carries a user-contributed biography (author Robert Stanley Ptaszek) that should not be relied on. It names Thomas's mother as 'Marie (Dubois)', lists children (John m. Sarah Holland, Samuel m. Martha Baker, Mary m. James Hicks, Jacob, Abigail, Rebecca...) that do not match Thomas's own 1815 will, has him moving to Luzerne 'about 1805' (he was in Plymouth by 1790 and in the 1800 census) and as a Luzerne justice 1813-17, and cites a 'Revolutionary-War Pension File NY-RWP-00123' showing a reduction to corporal in 1779. That citation is not in the form of a federal pension file number (S/W/R), no such pension appears in the indexes searched, and Thomas died in 1829, before the 1832 act under which most militia veterans applied ([R4-S1]). It should be treated as unsupported. Separately, the published New York in the Revolution (1898) lists Isaac Lamore, John Lamoreux and Nicolas Lamarux - but not Thomas - among the Orange County First Regiment land-bounty-rights men, alongside Benjamin and David Prindle ([R4-S2]).
